abstract:
  "The Diffusion Decision Model (DDM) decomposes response time and accuracy data from speeded decision-making tasks into latent cognitive parameters, including the rate of evidence accumulation, response caution, and non-decision time. The bmm R package provides three approaches for estimating DDM parameters that differ in data requirements, computational cost, and statistical assumptions: the EZ-Diffusion Model (summary-statistic approach), the Censored-Shifted Wald (single-boundary distributional approximation), and full DDM likelihood estimation via the Wiener first-passage time distribution. (2008), progressing from summary statistics to trial-level modeling. A cross-model comparison evaluates where the approaches agree and where they diverge.
```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| eval: true
pacman::p_load(here, bmm, brms, rtdists, tidyverse, tidybayes, patchwork)
source(here("functions", "clean_plot.R"))

# Load fitted models for real data
fit_acc_ezdm      <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc.rds"))
fit_resp_ezdm     <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp.rds"))
fit_cswald_simple <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_simple.rds"))
fit_cswald_resp   <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_resp.rds"))
fit_ddm_acc       <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_acc.rds"))
fit_ddm_resp      <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_resp.rds"))
fit_acc_ezdm_freq <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc_freq.rds"))
fit_resp_ezdm_freq <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp_freq.rds"))

# Load simulated models for appendix
fit_ezdm_3par    <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_3par.rds"))
fit_cswald_crisk <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_cswald_crisk.rds"))
fit_ddm          <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ddm.rds"))
true_params      <- read_csv(here("data", "true_parameters.csv"),
                              show_col_types = FALSE)
true_params_subject <- read_csv(here("data", "true_parameters_subject.csv"),
                                 show_col_types = FALSE)

# --- Extract inline reporting values ---

# Helper: format estimate with 95% CrI
fmt_est <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  sprintf("%.*f [%.*f, %.*f]", digits, x["Estimate"],
          digits, x["Q2.5"], digits, x["Q97.5"])
}

# Tutorial 1: EZDM 3par (accuracy-coded)
fe_t1 <- fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)
t1_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(fit_acc_ezdm), na.rm = TRUE)
t1_ess  <- min(summary(fit_acc_ezdm)$fixed[, "Bulk_ESS"], na.rm = TRUE)
t1_drift_word    <- fmt_est(fe_t1["drift_stim_catword", ])
t1_drift_nonword <- fmt_est(fe_t1["drift_stim_catnonword", ])
t1_bound_speed   <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t1["bound_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t1_bound_acc     <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t1["bound_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t1_ndt           <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t1["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t1_hyp_drift <- hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm, "drift_stim_catword > drift_stim_catnonword")
t1_bf_drift  <- t1_hyp_drift$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t1_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm, "bound_conditionaccuracy > bound_conditionspeed")
t1_bf_bound  <- t1_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio

# Tutorial 2: EZDM 4par (response-coded)
fe_t2 <- fixef(fit_resp_ezdm)
t2_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(fit_resp_ezdm), na.rm = TRUE)
t2_drift_word    <- fmt_est(fe_t2["drift_stim_catword", ])
t2_drift_nonword <- fmt_est(fe_t2["drift_stim_catnonword", ])
t2_zr_speed <- round(plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Estimate"]), 3)
t2_zr_acc   <- round(plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Estimate"]), 3)
t2_zr_speed_ci <- sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]",
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Estimate"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Q2.5"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Q97.5"]))
t2_zr_acc_ci <- sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]",
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Estimate"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Q2.5"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Q97.5"]))

# Tutorial 2: Hypothesis tests
t2_hyp_drift_word <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, "drift_stim_catword > 0")
t2_bf_drift_word  <- t2_hyp_drift_word$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t2_hyp_drift_nw   <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, "drift_stim_catnonword < 0")
t2_bf_drift_nw    <- t2_hyp_drift_nw$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t2_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, "bound_conditionaccuracy > bound_conditionspeed")
t2_bf_bound  <- t2_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio

# Tutorial 3: CSWALD simple + crisk
fe_t3s <- fixef(fit_cswald_simple)
fe_t3c <- fixef(fit_cswald_resp)
t3_rhat_simple <- max(brms::rhat(fit_cswald_simple), na.rm = TRUE)
t3_rhat_crisk  <- max(brms::rhat(fit_cswald_resp), na.rm = TRUE)
t3s_drift_word    <- fmt_est(fe_t3s["drift_stim_catword", ])
t3s_drift_nonword <- fmt_est(fe_t3s["drift_stim_catnonword", ])
t3s_bound_acc   <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t3s["bound_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t3s_bound_speed <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t3s["bound_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t3c_zr_speed <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t3c["zr_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t3c_zr_acc   <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t3c["zr_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
# Tutorial 3: Hypothesis tests
t3_hyp_drift <- hypothesis(fit_cswald_simple, "drift_stim_catword > drift_stim_catnonword")
t3_bf_drift  <- t3_hyp_drift$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t3_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_cswald_simple, "bound_conditionaccuracy > bound_conditionspeed")
t3_bf_bound  <- t3_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio

# Tutorial 4: DDM
fe_t4a <- fixef(fit_ddm_acc)
fe_t4r <- fixef(fit_ddm_resp)
t4_rhat_acc  <- max(brms::rhat(fit_ddm_acc), na.rm = TRUE)
t4_rhat_resp <- max(brms::rhat(fit_ddm_resp), na.rm = TRUE)
t4_drift_hf  <- round(fe_t4a["drift_freqhigh", "Estimate"], 2)
t4_drift_lf  <- round(fe_t4a["drift_freqlow", "Estimate"], 2)
t4_drift_vlf <- round(fe_t4a["drift_freqvery_low", "Estimate"], 2)
t4_drift_nw  <- round(fe_t4a["drift_freqnonword", "Estimate"], 2)
t4_bound_acc   <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["bound_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t4_bound_speed <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["bound_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t4_ndt <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_zr_speed <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t4r["zr_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_zr_acc   <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t4r["zr_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)

# Tutorial 4: Hypothesis tests (parallel to Tutorials 1-3)
t4_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_ddm_acc, "bound_conditionaccuracy > bound_conditionspeed")
t4_bf_bound  <- t4_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t4_hyp_drift <- hypothesis(fit_ddm_acc, "drift_freqhigh > drift_freqvery_low")
t4_bf_drift  <- t4_hyp_drift$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio

# Tutorial 4: EZ-Diffusion (freq) vs full DDM divergences
fe_t4f   <- fixef(fit_acc_ezdm_freq)
t4_ndt_ez  <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4f["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_ndt_ddm <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
.drift_lvls   <- c("freqhigh", "freqlow", "freqvery_low", "freqnonword")
.drift_ratios <- fe_t4f[paste0("drift_", .drift_lvls), "Estimate"] /
                 fe_t4a[paste0("drift_", .drift_lvls), "Estimate"]
t4_drift_pct_mean <- round((mean(.drift_ratios) - 1) * 100)
t4_drift_pct_lo   <- round((min(.drift_ratios) - 1) * 100)
t4_drift_pct_hi   <- round((max(.drift_ratios) - 1) * 100)

# Appendix: Subject-level recovery correlations
extract_subject_params <- function(fit, model_name, n_subjects = 50) {
  co <- coef(fit)$id
  bind_rows(
    tibble(model = model_name, parameter = "drift_easy",
           id = 1:n_subjects, recovered = co[1:n_subjects, "Estimate", "drift_conditioneasy"]),
    tibble(model = model_name, parameter = "drift_hard",
           id = 1:n_subjects, recovered = co[1:n_subjects, "Estimate", "drift_conditionhard"]),
    tibble(model = model_name, parameter = "bound",
           id = 1:n_subjects, recovered = exp(co[1:n_subjects, "Estimate", "bound_Intercept"])),
    tibble(model = model_name, parameter = "ndt",
           id = 1:n_subjects, recovered = exp(co[1:n_subjects, "Estimate", "ndt_Intercept"]))
  )
}

subject_recovery <- bind_rows(
  extract_subject_params(fit_ezdm_3par, "EZDM 3par"),
  extract_subject_params(fit_cswald_crisk, "CSWALD crisk"),
  extract_subject_params(fit_ddm, "DDM")
)

true_subject <- bind_rows(
  true_params_subject |> filter(condition == "easy") |> transmute(id, parameter = "drift_easy", true_value = drift_subj),
  true_params_subject |> filter(condition == "hard") |> transmute(id, parameter = "drift_hard", true_value = drift_subj),
  true_params_subject |> filter(condition == "easy") |> transmute(id, parameter = "bound", true_value = bound_subj),
  true_params_subject |> filter(condition == "easy") |> transmute(id, parameter = "ndt", true_value = ndt_subj)
)

subject_recovery <- subject_recovery |>
  left_join(true_subject, by = c("id", "parameter"))

recovery_cors <- subject_recovery |>
  group_by(model, parameter) |>
  summarise(r = cor(true_value, recovered), .groups = "drop")

recovery_r_min <- round(min(recovery_cors$r), 2)
recovery_r_max <- round(max(recovery_cors$r), 2)
recovery_r_median <- round(median(recovery_cors$r), 2)
```

# Introduction

Consider two participants performing a speeded choice task, for example deciding if a digit is odd or even as quickly and accurately as possible. Participant A responds in 550 ms on average with 90% accuracy; Participant B responds in 600 ms with 95% accuracy. Who did better on the task? A traditional analysis might favor A (faster) or B (more accurate), depending which indicator to weigh more strongly, but neither summary statistic alone can determine *why* and *how* these participants differ on the level of the underlying cognitive processes. Participant A may extract evidence faster but set a more liberal decision threshold, while Participant B may extract evidence at the same rate but set a more cautious threshold that trades speed for accuracy. Mean RT and accuracy alone cannot distinguish these accounts — they confound different underlying processes.

Evidence accumulation models (EAMs) resolve this ambiguity. By jointly modeling response times (RTs) and accuracy from speeded decision-making tasks, EAMs decompose observed performance into latent cognitive parameters: the rate of evidence accumulation (drift), the amount of evidence required before responding (boundary separation), and the time consumed by non-decisional processes such as stimulus encoding and motor execution (non-decision time). Since their introduction [@ratcliff1978theory], EAMs have become the standard framework for analyzing RT data across perception, memory retrieval, and cognitive control [@ratcliff2008diffusion; @donkin2018response; @evans2019evidence].

The EAM family encompasses a range of model architectures. In *race models*, separate accumulators independently accumulate evidence for each response option, with the first to reach threshold determining the response — examples include the Linear Ballistic Accumulator [LBA; @brown2008lba], the lognormal race model [@rouder2015lnr], and the racing diffusion model [@tillman2020racing]. In *competitive models* such as the Leaky Competing Accumulator [LCA; @usher2001lca], accumulators mutually inhibit each other, producing dynamics that can account for contextual effects in multi-alternative choice. These architectures share the same core logic — noisy evidence accumulation toward a decision threshold — but differ in whether accumulation is deterministic or stochastic, whether accumulators interact, and how many response options can be modeled [for reviews, see @ratcliff2004comparison; @forstmann2016review; @boag2025expert]. Among these, the Diffusion Decision Model [DDM; @ratcliff1978theory] is the most widely applied EAM for two-choice tasks, supported by decades of empirical validation across cognitive domains [@ratcliff2008diffusion].

Within the DDM framework, multiple estimation approaches exist that differ in data requirements, computational cost, and statistical assumptions [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion; @anders2016shifted; @ratcliff1978theory; @vandekerckhove2007fitting]. All estimate the same DDM parameters — drift, boundary separation, non-decision time, and (optionally) relative starting point — but they extract these parameters from data at different levels of granularity: from aggregated summary statistics, from trial-level RT distributions using distributional approximations, or from the full Wiener first-passage time likelihood. Choosing among these approaches involves navigating trade-offs that are compounded by the fact that RT data routinely contain contaminant processes (fast guesses, attentional lapses) that bias parameter estimates [@ratcliff2021methods; @boag2025expert]. Until recently, each approach required its own specialized software, making cross-approach comparison difficult. The `bmm` R package [@popov2024bmm] addresses this by implementing three DDM estimation approaches — the EZ-Diffusion Model [`ezdm` in `bmm`; @wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion], the Censored-Shifted Wald [`cswald`; @anders2016shifted], and full DDM likelihood estimation [`ddm`] — within a unified Bayesian hierarchical framework built on `brms` [@burkner2017brms] and Stan [@cmdstanr2024]. The consistent interface means that switching between estimation approaches requires changing only the model object, while the formula syntax, prior specification, and post-processing tools remain identical.[^future]

[^future]: The implementation of race-model architectures in `bmm` may follow in future versions of the package.

Estimating DDM parameters within a Bayesian hierarchical framework offers several advantages over the single-subject maximum likelihood approaches that dominated earlier work. Hierarchical estimation borrows strength across participants, producing more stable individual-level estimates even with moderate trial counts — a common practical constraint in multi-condition designs. It provides proper uncertainty quantification through posterior distributions rather than point estimates, and it naturally handles the unbalanced cell sizes that arise when some conditions produce few errors. Furthermore, a unified interface for all three estimation approaches makes cross-approach comparison straightforward: because the formula syntax, prior specification, and post-processing tools are identical, researchers can fit all three approaches and directly compare their conclusions. As we demonstrate in this tutorial, the Bayesian hierarchical formulation also transforms the EZ-Diffusion Model — originally designed as a quick approximation — into a viable primary analysis tool that produces substantively identical drift-related conclusions to the full DDM at a fraction of the computational cost.

This tutorial is written for researchers with basic familiarity with R and `brms` who have collected or plan to collect two-choice RT data. After completing the tutorials, you will be able to:

1. Preprocess RT data to detect and handle contaminant responses using `bmm`'s dedicated tools.
2. Specify, fit, and evaluate DDM-based models using the `ezdm`, `cswald`, and `ddm` implementations in `bmm`.
3. Choose among estimation approaches and apply them to empirical data.

The tutorial focuses on the simple (four-parameter) DDM framework for two-choice tasks. It does not cover the full DDM with between-trial variability parameters, race-model architectures (e.g., the LBA or racing diffusion model), multi-alternative choice tasks, or formal model comparison techniques such as leave-one-out cross-validation or bridge sampling — these are available via `brms` but beyond the present scope.

We begin with a data preprocessing section demonstrating how contaminants bias DDM parameter estimates (using simulated data with known ground truth) and introducing `bmm`'s preprocessing tools. We then introduce the empirical dataset — the classic lexical decision study by @wagenmakers2008lexical — which serves as the running example for all subsequent tutorials. Four tutorials progressively apply the EZ-Diffusion Model, Censored-Shifted Wald, and full DDM to this dataset, each motivated by a limitation of the previous approach, followed by a cross-approach comparison and practical guidelines. A short simulated parameter recovery study at both group and individual level is provided in the Appendix. Complete R scripts are available on OSF and GitHub [see also @frischkorn2025tutorial for a companion tutorial on mixture models in `bmm`; @boag2025expert for experimental design guidance].

# Background: Evidence Accumulation Models

## The Diffusion Model Framework

To build intuition for what EAMs capture, consider a concrete example. A participant in a lexical decision task sees the letter string CHAIR on screen and must press one of two buttons to indicate "word" or "nonword." Upon stimulus onset, the participant begins extracting evidence — orthographic regularity, phonological plausibility, lexical familiarity — that accumulates noisily over time toward one of two response boundaries. If the accumulated evidence reaches the "word" boundary first, the participant responds "word"; if it reaches the "nonword" boundary, they respond "nonword." The observed RT is the sum of this decision time and non-decisional components (for example, stimulus encoding and motor execution). This example reflects the core logic of the DDM [@ratcliff1978theory; @ratcliff2008diffusion], and it gives rise to four parameters that each capture a distinct aspect of the decision process:

- **Drift** ($\delta$): The mean rate of evidence accumulation, reflecting stimulus quality or strength. Higher drift yields faster and more accurate responses.
- **Boundary Separation** ($\alpha$): The distance between the two response boundaries, capturing *response caution*. Wider boundaries require more evidence, yielding slower but more accurate responses.
- **Non-decision Time** ($\tau$): The portion of the observed RT not attributable to the decision process, encompassing *stimulus encoding* and *motor execution*.
- **Relative Starting Point** ($\zeta_r$): The position of the starting point between the two boundaries, expressed as a proportion (0.5 = unbiased). Values deviating from 0.5 indicate an *a priori response bias*.
  
```{r}
#| label: fig-diffusion-schematic
#| fig-cap: "Schematic of the Diffusion Decision Model. Evidence accumulates noisily from a starting point ($\\zeta_r$) toward one of two response boundaries separated by distance $\\alpha$. The mean rate of accumulation is the drift ($\\delta$). The non-decision time ($\\tau$, shaded region) captures stimulus encoding and motor execution. Two example paths are shown: one reaching the upper boundary (correct response, blue) and one reaching the lower boundary (error response, red)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "03_diffusion_schematic.pdf"))
```

These parameters are not merely mathematical abstractions — they make testable predictions about how experimental manipulations should affect behavior. According to the principle of *selective influence*, manipulations designed to affect a specific cognitive process should primarily change the corresponding model parameter while leaving the others relatively unchanged. For example, stimulus quality manipulations (e.g., degradation, word frequency) should affect drift, whereas *response caution* manipulations (e.g., speed–accuracy instructions) should affect bound [@voss2004interpreting; @ratcliff2008diffusion]. This selective influence, consistently demonstrated in previous studies, is a key motivation for using EAMs [see @boag2025expert, Table 2, for a comprehensive overview].

The four-parameter formulation of the DDM described above is sometimes called the *simple* or *pure* DDM. The *full* DDM [@ratcliff2002estimating] adds three trial-to-trial variability parameters: variability in drift (to produce slow errors), variability in starting point (to produce fast errors), and variability in ndt (to account for leading-edge variation in RT distributions). These additional parameters increase the model's flexibility but also its complexity and computational cost, while the added parameters are often difficult to recover reliably from data [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez; @boag2025expert]. For many applications — particularly when the goal is to detect condition effects on drift or boundary separation rather than to characterize the precise shape of error RT distributions — the simple DDM provides a more parsimonious and statistically powerful alternative [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. All three estimation approaches in `bmm` are based on the simple DDM framework.

## DDM Estimation Approaches in bmm

The `bmm` package implements three approaches for estimating DDM parameters that share the same theoretical framework but differ in data requirements and computational cost. @tbl-model-comparison summarizes the key differences.

| Feature | EZ-Diffusion Model | Censored-Shifted Wald | Full DDM |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `bmm` function | `ezdm()` | `cswald()` | `ddm()` |
| Data level | Aggregated | Trial-level | Trial-level |
| Input | Mean RT, Var RT, accuracy | RT, response | RT, response |
| Parameters | drift, bound, ndt (+zr in 4par) | drift, bound, ndt (+zr in crisk) | drift, bound, ndt (+zr) |
| Likelihood | Closed-form equations | Shifted Wald | Wiener first-passage time |
| Min trials/cell | ~30 | ~50 | ~50 |
| Starting point ($\zeta$) | 4par only | crisk only | Optional |
| Fitting time | Seconds–minutes | ~1–5 hours | ~15–20 hours |
| Best suited for | Exploration, many conditions | Iterative development | Confirmatory analysis |

: Summary of the three DDM estimation approaches in `bmm`. {#tbl-model-comparison}

### EZ-Diffusion Model

The EZ-Diffusion Model [`ezdm` in `bmm`; @wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion] was developed to make diffusion model analysis quick and easy by eliminating the need for iterative fitting routines [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion]. It provides closed-form expressions that map three summary statistics — mean RT, RT variance, and proportion correct — directly to drift, boundary separation, and non-decision time. This simplicity comes at the cost of two assumptions: no trial-to-trial variability in any parameter, and an unbiased starting point ($\zeta = 0.5$). When these assumptions are violated, parameter estimates can be attenuated — particularly drift at high values — but the model remains a surprisingly powerful tool for detecting condition effects, often outperforming the full DDM in statistical power [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez; @ratcliff2008ez; @wagenmakers2008extensions]. Several extensions address specific limitations: *robust-EZ* uses an ex-Gaussian/uniform mixture model to down-weight contaminant RTs before computing summary statistics [@wagenmakers2008extensions]; a four-parameter extension allows to estimate the relative starting point from boundary-specific RT moments, building on generalized expressions for the mean and variance of decision times under the diffusion model with biased starting point [@grasman2009ez; @srivastava2016moments]; Crucially, a recent Bayesian hierarchical formulation casts the EZ-Diffusion equations as a probabilistic proxy model, enabling hierarchical estimation with regression structures on parameters [@chavez2025ez].

### Censored-Shifted Wald Model

The EZ-Diffusion Model's speed comes from working with summary statistics, but this means it cannot incorporate trial-level predictors or preserve information about the shape of the RT distribution. The full DDM preserves all of this but is computationally expensive. The Censored-Shifted Wald [`cswald` in `bmm`; @anders2016shifted] offers a middle path: it models individual RTs directly — preserving distributional information and enabling trial-level predictors — while remaining substantially faster than the full DDM.

The Censored-Shifted Wald achieves this by using the shifted Wald (inverse Gaussian) distribution, which describes the first-passage time of a diffusion process to a single absorbing boundary [@anders2016shifted]. This is a simpler process than the two-boundary framework of the DDM, and therefore faster to evaluate. Crucially, when error rates are low — due to high drift, wide bound, or a response bias toward the correct boundary — the shifted Wald parameters closely approximate those of the full Wiener distribution that underlies the DDM [@miller2018shifted]. In other words, when most responses are correct, the decision process behaves as if there were effectively only one boundary to reach, and the Censored-Shifted Wald captures this well.

Two versions implemented in `bmm` handle error responses differently. The *simple* version treats errors as *censored* correct responses using survival analysis techniques — appropriate when error rates are below approximately 20% [@miller2018shifted]. The *competing-risks* (crisk) version models both correct and error RTs through two independent racing shifted Wald processes with shared ndt, additionally estimating the relative starting point. At higher error rates or when response bias is of interest, the competing-risks version provides a better approximation to the full Wiener likelihood [@miller2018shifted].

### Full DDM Likelihood Estimation

The full DDM estimation approach [`ddm` in `bmm`] uses the Wiener first-passage time distribution, which jointly models both the RT and the response boundary that was reached [@ratcliff1978theory; @vandekerckhove2007fitting]. Unlike the Censored-Shifted Wald, which approximates the decision process with one or two independent single-boundary accumulators, the full DDM models the two-boundary process directly. This means it simultaneously captures the probability of reaching each boundary *and* the complete distribution of times to reach it — making it the mathematically most accurate and complete characterization of the evidence accumulation process within a single likelihood function. However, evaluating the Wiener density involves an infinite series that must be truncated adaptively, making likelihood computation substantially more expensive than for the `ezdm` or `cswald` approaches [@navarro2009fast]. Various estimation methods have been developed over the years, including chi-square fitting [@ratcliff2002estimating], maximum likelihood [@vandekerckhove2007fitting; @voss2007fastdm], and hierarchical Bayesian methods [@vandekerckhove2011hierarchical; @wiecki2013hddm]. In `bmm`, the full DDM is fitted via Stan's `wiener_lpdf()` function, which implements efficient series truncation within a fully Bayesian hierarchical framework.

## Contaminant Processes in RT Data

Not all observed RTs arise from the evidence accumulation process that EAMs are designed to characterize. *Fast guesses* — responses emitted before meaningful stimulus evaluation — produce RTs below what any accumulation-to-bound process could generate, with accuracy near chance. *Slow outliers* result from attentional lapses or distraction, producing abnormally long RTs that inflate RT variance. Both violate the core assumption that each observed RT reflects a decision time plus non-decision time [@ratcliff2002estimating; @ratcliff2021methods]. Even moderate contamination rates (3–5%) can substantially bias EAM parameter estimates [@ratcliff1993methods; @ulrich1994effects]. The next section demonstrates the magnitude of this problem using simulation and introduces `bmm`'s tools for addressing it.

# Data Preprocessing: Principles and Tools

Data preprocessing is not merely a housekeeping step — it is a substantive methodological decision that directly affects parameter estimates. A common approach is to apply hard RT cutoffs (e.g., removing all RTs below 200 ms or above 3,000 ms), but such cutoffs are arbitrary and can themselves introduce bias by removing legitimate fast or slow responses. The `bmm` package provides a principled, model-based alternative: a mixture-model approach that separates contaminant responses from the core decision process probabilistically. In this section, we demonstrate the severity of contaminant bias using simulation and then introduce `bmm`'s preprocessing tools.^[The companion scripts `scripts/10_tutorial0_data_preprocessing.R` and `scripts/02_simulation_contaminant_methods.R` contain the full code for all analyses in this section.]

## Demonstrating Contaminant Bias

To illustrate the severity of contaminant bias under controlled conditions, we use simulated data generated from a DDM with known parameters (drift: 2.5 for an easy, 1.0 for a hard condition; bound: 1.5; ndt: 0.3) for 50 participants, each completing 200 trials per condition. We then inject contaminant responses — 4% fast guesses (uniform RTs between 0.05 and ndt with 50% accuracy) and 3% slow outliers (uniform RTs between the 95th percentile and 2 times the maximum RT) — to produce a contaminated version of the same dataset.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rt-density
#| fig-cap: "Density plots of reaction time distributions for clean and contaminated data by condition. Contaminated data show heavier tails on both ends due to injected fast guesses and slow outliers."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "10_rt_density.pdf"))
```

@fig-rt-density shows visible tails on both ends of the contaminated RT distributions. @fig-sumstats-bias shows the downstream impact: contaminated data produce inflated RT variance, shifted mean RT, and reduced accuracy. Because EZ-Diffusion parameters are direct transformations of these summary statistics, any distortion propagates directly to biased parameter estimates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sumstats-bias
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of summary statistics (mean RT, variance of RT, accuracy) computed from contaminated versus clean data. Each box spans the interquartile range across 50 simulated participants. Contaminant responses inflate RT variance, shift mean RT, and reduce accuracy."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "10_sumstats_bias.pdf"))
```

## Identifying Contaminant Responses with `flag_contaminant_rts()`

The `flag_contaminant_rts()` function implements a mixture-model approach: within each participant × condition cell, an EM algorithm decomposes the RT distribution into a core component (ex-Gaussian, lognormal, or inverse Gaussian) and a uniform contaminant component, returning the posterior probability that each trial is a contaminant.

```{r}
#| label: flag-contaminant
data_flagged <- data_contaminated |>
  group_by(id, condition) |>
  mutate(
    contam_prob = flag_contaminant_rts(
      rt,
      distribution = "exgaussian",
      contaminant_bound = c("min", "max")
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```

Trials with `contam_prob > 0.5` are classified as likely contaminants — the 0.5 threshold represents a natural decision boundary: trials above this value are more likely to be contaminants than legitimate responses according to the mixture model. In a companion Monte Carlo simulation (4,500 datasets varying the contamination rate from 0% to 10%), the ex-Gaussian mixture achieved consistently high classification performance, with F1 scores above 0.85 even at 10% contamination.^[`validate_fast_guesses()` provides a principled check that flagged fast trials actually show random guessing behavior by computing a Bayes Factor for H0: accuracy = 0.5 among flagged trials.]

When using contaminant probabilities to exclude trials before trial-level model fitting (`cswald`, `ddm`), two approaches are available. *Threshold-based flagging* excludes all trials above a fixed cutoff (typically `contam_prob > 0.5`). This is deterministic and straightforward, but treats a trial with `contam_prob = 0.51` identically to one with `contam_prob = 0.99`. *Probabilistic flagging* instead draws a Bernoulli variable for each trial using the contaminant probability as the exclusion rate: `rbinom(n, 1, contam_prob)`. Trials with high contaminant probability are very likely excluded, while borderline trials have a proportional chance of retention — better reflecting the uncertainty in the classification. The companion script compares both approaches; in practice, they yield similar results for well-separated contaminant distributions, but probabilistic flagging is more principled when contaminant probabilities cluster near the decision boundary. For `ezdm` fitting, neither approach is needed — the mixture method in `ezdm_summary_stats()` handles contaminants directly through down-weighting.

## Computing Summary Statistics with `ezdm_summary_stats()`

For `ezdm` fitting, raw trial-level data must be aggregated into summary statistics. The `ezdm_summary_stats()` function provides three aggregation methods: `simple` (standard mean and variance), `robust` (MAD-based estimators), and `mixture` (EM-weighted aggregation that down-weights contaminant trials). The mixture method integrates contaminant detection and summary statistic computation into a single step.

```{r}
#| label: ezdm-sumstats
data_sumstats <- data_contaminated |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(
      rt, response,
      version  = "3par",
      method   = "mixture",
      distribution = "exgaussian"
    ),
    .by = c(id, condition)
  )
```

This produces one row per participant per condition, with columns for mean RT, RT variance, and trial counts — the inputs the EZ-Diffusion Model requires. The `mixture` method handles contaminant detection and aggregation in a single step: rather than first excluding outliers and then computing statistics, it simultaneously estimates the core distribution's mean and variance while down-weighting contaminant contributions. But how well does this work in practice?

## Comparing Preprocessing Methods

@fig-simulation-methods presents the Monte Carlo simulation results, comparing median absolute error (MAE) in recovered summary statistics across preprocessing methods and contamination rates. The mixture method with ex-Gaussian distribution consistently achieves the lowest overall MAE, reducing error in RT variance by approximately 90% compared to naive aggregation at 10% contamination. The robust method also substantially reduces variance error but shows a distinct profile that warrants discussion.

```{r}
#| label: fig-simulation-methods
#| fig-cap: "Monte Carlo simulation results (500 replications per condition). Median absolute error of recovered summary statistics across five preprocessing methods and six total contamination rates (0–10%). The mixture method with ex-Gaussian distribution (blue, thick line) consistently achieves the lowest error. The robust method (yellow) performs well for RT variance but shows elevated error for mean RT."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "02_method_comparison.pdf"))
```

A targeted simulation varying population ndt reveals a fundamental trade-off between the methods (@fig-prefilter-ndt). The robust method (MAD-based estimators) recovers RT variance with the lowest error across all ndt values and is insensitive to hard pre-filtering. However, it systematically overestimates mean RT — an inherent property of median-based location estimators applied to right-skewed distributions. Because EZ-Diffusion parameters are derived from these summary statistics through closed-form equations, this bias has a specific and predictable consequence: drift and bound, which are computed from RT variance and accuracy, remain unaffected, but ndt — which is computed as mean RT minus estimated decision time — absorbs the entire mean RT bias, producing systematically inflated ndt estimates. The mixture method avoids this by simultaneously estimating the core distribution's mean and variance while separating out contaminant contributions, yielding accurate recovery of both summary statistics and, consequently, all three EZ-Diffusion parameters.

```{r}
#| label: fig-prefilter-ndt
#| fig-cap: "Method comparison across population non-decision time values at 10% total contamination. Left: Mean RT error — the robust method (yellow) shows consistently elevated MAE due to median-based location estimation on right-skewed distributions. The mixture method (blue) improves with increasing ndt. Right: Var RT error — the robust method achieves the lowest MAE, flat across ndt values. Hard pre-filtering (dashed lines) degrades mixture performance but does not affect the robust method."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "02_prefilter_ndt.pdf"))
```

Based on these results, we recommend the **mixture method** with ex-Gaussian distribution as the default for `ezdm` preprocessing, as it provides accurate recovery of all summary statistics and, by extension, all EZ-Diffusion parameters. The **robust method** is a useful alternative when the mixture model's EM algorithm cannot converge — for example, in cells with very few trials (see Tutorial 4) — with the understanding that ndt estimates will be biased upward. In either case, hard pre-filtering (removing all RTs below a fixed cutoff) is unnecessary and actively harmful: it increases MAE for the mixture method by 60–74% at short ndt, where fixed cutoffs remove legitimate fast responses alongside genuine contaminants. All subsequent tutorials use the mixture method as the default, with the robust method applied where cell sizes are too small for EM convergence.

## Validation Against Published Exclusion Criteria

The simulation above demonstrates that the mixture method works under controlled conditions where the ground truth is known. But does it also work on real data, where the true contamination rate is unknown? We can validate the approach against the exclusion criteria used in the original @wagenmakers2008lexical study, which excluded trials with RT < 180 ms or RT > 3000 ms — a standard hard-cutoff approach. When we apply `flag_contaminant_rts()` to the full dataset (including the trials that the original study excluded), the mixture model catches 91.5% of the trials flagged by the hard cutoffs. The 14 missed trials fall just below the 0.5 threshold (contaminant probabilities of 0.30–0.49), representing borderline cases near the hard cutoff boundaries. More importantly, the mixture model additionally flags 143 trials *within* the 180 ms–3 s range that the hard cutoffs miss entirely — trials with abnormally long RTs (median: 2.1 s) that the mixture model identifies as distributional outliers based on the shape of the RT distribution. This demonstrates that the mixture approach is strictly more informative than hard cutoffs: it recovers nearly all the same exclusions while detecting additional outliers that fixed thresholds cannot identify.

# The Lexical Decision Dataset

With the preprocessing toolkit established, we now turn to the empirical dataset that serves as the running example for all tutorials. We use the classic lexical decision study by @wagenmakers2008lexical, available as `speed_acc` in the `rtdists` R package [@singmann2016rtdists]. This dataset is ideal for a tutorial for several reasons: it is publicly available and widely used as a benchmark in the diffusion modeling literature, its experimental design has clear and well-tested EAM predictions, and published parameter estimates from the original analysis provide reference values for validating our results.

In this experiment, 17 participants classified letter strings as words or nonwords under two instruction conditions: *speed emphasis* (respond as quickly as possible) and *accuracy emphasis* (respond as accurately as possible). Stimuli included words of varying frequency (high, low, very low) and matched nonwords, creating a 2 (emphasis) × 2 (stimulus category) within-subjects design with approximately 460 trials per cell per participant.

This design maps cleanly onto EAM predictions. According to the *selective influence* principle, speed–accuracy emphasis should primarily affect bound (response caution), while stimulus category should primarily affect drift (evidence quality — words produce stronger lexical evidence than nonwords).

## Data Preparation

We load the data, convert factors to character (needed because `response` and `stim_cat` have different factor level sets), and remove the 6 recording failures and all censored trials.

```{r}
#| label: data-load
data("speed_acc", package = "rtdists")

data_lexical <- speed_acc |>
  mutate(
    response = as.character(response),
    stim_cat = as.character(stim_cat),
    condition = factor(condition, levels = c("speed", "accuracy"))
  ) |>
  filter(response != "error", censor == FALSE)
```

For EAMs, the response variable must be binary, indicating which of the two decision boundaries was reached. Two codings are possible, each answering a different question:

- **Accuracy-coded** (upper = correct, lower = error): Drift reflects how quickly evidence for the *correct answer* accumulates. This is the standard approach for testing selective influence.
- **Response-coded** (upper = "word" response, lower = "nonword" response): Drift reflects evidence toward saying *"word"* specifically — positive for word stimuli, negative or near zero for nonwords. The relative starting point ($\zeta$) captures response bias toward saying "word."

```{r}
#| label: data-recode
# Accuracy-coded: correct = upper, error = lower
data_accuracy <- data_lexical |>
  mutate(response = ifelse(response == stim_cat, "upper", "lower"))

# Response-coded: "word" response = upper, "nonword" response = lower
data_response <- data_lexical |>
  mutate(response = ifelse(response == "word", "upper", "lower"))
```

We apply contaminant detection and compute summary statistics for the EZ-Diffusion tutorials.

```{r}
#| label: data-preprocess
# Flag contaminant trials
data_accuracy <- data_accuracy |>
  group_by(id, condition, stim_cat) |>
  mutate(
    contam_prob = flag_contaminant_rts(
      rt, distribution = "exgaussian",
      contaminant_bound = c("min", "max")
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Clean trial-level data (for CSWALD/DDM)
data_accuracy_clean <- data_accuracy |> filter(contam_prob <= 0.5)
data_response_clean <- data_response |>
  semi_join(data_accuracy_clean, by = c("id", "condition", "stim_cat", "rt"))

# EZDM 3par summary statistics (accuracy-coded)
data_acc_ezdm <- data_accuracy |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(rt, response, version = "3par",
                       method = "mixture", distribution = "exgaussian"),
    .by = c(id, condition, stim_cat)
  )

# EZDM 4par summary statistics (response-coded)
data_resp_ezdm <- data_response |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(rt, response, version = "4par",
                       method = "mixture", distribution = "exgaussian"),
    .by = c(id, condition, stim_cat)
  )
```

# Tutorial 1: Exploring Condition Effects with the EZ-Diffusion Model

Let's start with the simplest and fastest DDM estimation approach in `bmm`: the EZ-Diffusion Model (`ezdm`). Because it fits in seconds rather than hours, it is the natural first step for exploring condition effects. The central question is: *Do speed–accuracy emphasis and stimulus category selectively influence different cognitive parameters?*^[The companion script `scripts/11_tutorial1_ezdm_3par.R` contains the full executable code for this tutorial.]

## Model Specification

Specifying an EAM in `bmm` involves two objects: a model object that defines the measurement model and maps data columns to model components, and a formula object that specifies the predictor structure for each parameter. The `ezdm()` function creates the model object:

```{r}
#| label: t1-model
model_acc <- ezdm(
  mean_rt  = "mean_rt",
  var_rt   = "var_rt",
  n_upper  = "n_upper",
  n_trials = "n_trials",
  version  = "3par"
)
```

The formula is specified using `bmf()`, which allows separate regression formulas for each parameter. We include stimulus category as a predictor on drift (to test for evidence quality differences) and emphasis condition as a predictor on bound (to test for response caution differences). Random slopes allow each participant's parameters to vary by condition: `(0 + stim_cat | id)` estimates participant-specific drift for words and nonwords, while `(0 + condition | id)` estimates participant-specific boundary settings under speed and accuracy emphasis.

Each parameter uses a *link function* that determines how the linear predictor maps onto the parameter scale. Drift can take any real value — positive when evidence favors the upper boundary, negative when it favors the lower boundary — so it uses an *identity link*, meaning the regression coefficients are directly on the drift scale. Boundary separation and non-decision time, by contrast, must be strictly positive (a negative boundary or negative encoding time is meaningless), so they use a *log link*: the regression coefficients are on the log scale and must be exponentiated to obtain the parameter estimate. This is analogous to using a log link in Poisson regression to ensure predicted counts are positive. In practice, this means that when interpreting `fixef()` output, drift coefficients can be read directly, while bound and ndt coefficients require exponentiation (we demonstrate this below).

```{r}
#| label: t1-formula
formula_acc <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stim_cat + (0 + stim_cat | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
```

We use `bmm`'s default priors, which are moderately informative and appropriate for typical experimental data. Custom priors can be inspected via `default_prior(formula_acc, data_acc_ezdm, model_acc)` and overridden using `brms::prior()`. For researchers who want to verify that their priors produce plausible predictions before seeing the data, `bmm` supports prior predictive checks via `bmm(... sample_prior = "only")`, which generates data from the prior alone. We omit this step here because the default priors have been calibrated for typical RT data, but it is recommended practice when specifying custom priors (see Practical Guidelines).

## Model Fitting

The model is fitted using `bmm()`, which wraps `brms::brm()` with model-specific likelihoods. Setting `sample_prior = "yes"` enables prior-vs.-posterior comparisons; `file` caches the fitted model to disk.

```{r}
#| label: t1-fit
fit_acc_ezdm <- bmm(
  formula = formula_acc,
  data    = data_acc_ezdm,
  model   = model_acc,
  chains  = 5,
  cores   = 5,
  warmup  = 1000,
  iter    = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12),
  file    = here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc")
)
```

Fitting completed in approximately 30 seconds with 5 parallel chains. Convergence should always be verified before interpreting results. The two key diagnostics are $\hat{R}$ (which should be below 1.01 for all parameters) and effective sample size (ESS, which should be at least 400 for reliable posterior summaries). Both can be inspected via `summary(fit_acc_ezdm)`, which displays these diagnostics for every parameter. For this model, the maximum $\hat{R}$ was `r round(t1_rhat, 3)` and the minimum bulk ESS was `r round(t1_ess)`, indicating that the chains mixed well and the posterior was adequately sampled.^[If convergence issues arise, standard remedies include increasing the number of iterations, raising `adapt_delta` (e.g., to 0.95 or 0.99), or simplifying the random-effects structure. See the Troubleshooting section in Practical Guidelines for details.]

## Model Evaluation

Before interpreting parameter estimates, we verify model fit via a posterior predictive check (@fig-t1-ppcheck), which overlays response-time distributions simulated from the posterior on the observed distributions; close overlap across both the bulk and the tails indicates that the model reproduces the data it was fit to. One caveat is specific to the EZ-Diffusion Model: because it is fit to three summary statistics per cell rather than to individual RTs, its posterior predictive check can only confirm that those moments — mean RT, RT variance, and accuracy — are recovered, and cannot detect misfit in the finer shape of the RT distribution. The trial-level Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM, which model individual RTs (including the separate distributions of correct and error responses), yield more diagnostic checks; we return to these in Tutorials 3 and 4.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check for the EZ-Diffusion 3-parameter model fitted to the Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data. Close overlap between observed (dark) and predicted (light) distributions indicates adequate model fit."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "11_pp_check.pdf"))
```

Parameter estimates are extracted on their natural scales using `fixef()`. For drift (identity link), estimates are directly interpretable. For bound and ndt (log links), estimates must be exponentiated.

```{r}
#| label: t1-params
# Population-level estimates
fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)

# Transform to natural scale
exp(fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)["bound_conditionspeed", ])
exp(fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)["bound_conditionaccuracy", ])
```

The `fixef()` output shows the population-level regression coefficients. For drift (identity link), the `Estimate` column is directly on the drift scale — for instance, a value of 3.5 means a drift of 3.5. For bound and ndt (log link), the estimates are on the log scale: the `exp()` transformation converts them to the natural scale. For example, a log-scale bound estimate of 0.4 corresponds to a boundary separation of $e^{0.4} \approx 1.49$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-params
#| fig-cap: "EZ-Diffusion parameter estimates from the accuracy-coded analysis. Left: Drift estimates by stimulus category — word stimuli produce higher drift than nonword stimuli, reflecting stronger lexical evidence. Right: Bound estimates by emphasis condition — speed emphasis produces lower boundary separation, reflecting reduced response caution."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "11_param_estimates.pdf"))
```

The results reveal a clear double dissociation consistent with selective influence (@fig-t1-params). Stimulus category selectively influenced drift — word stimuli produced higher drift ($\delta$ = `r t1_drift_word`) than nonword stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t1_drift_nonword`), reflecting stronger lexical evidence for real words. Emphasis condition selectively influenced bound — speed emphasis produced lower boundary separation ($\alpha$ = `r t1_bound_speed`) than accuracy emphasis ($\alpha$ = `r t1_bound_acc`), reflecting reduced response caution. Non-decision time was estimated at $\tau$ = `r t1_ndt` seconds. This dissociation demonstrates the core value of EAMs: a traditional analysis comparing mean RTs could not distinguish whether speed-emphasis participants were faster because they processed evidence more efficiently or because they required less evidence. We return to this pattern in Tutorial 4, where we show that the EZ-Diffusion Model produces substantively identical drift-related conclusions to the computationally much more expensive full DDM.

## Hypothesis Testing

Because we fitted the model with `sample_prior = "yes"`, we can use `brms::hypothesis()` to test directed hypotheses via Savage-Dickey density ratios:

```{r}
#| label: t1-hypothesis
# Test: drift higher for words than nonwords
hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm, "drift_stim_catword > drift_stim_catnonword")

# Test: bound higher for accuracy than speed emphasis
hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm, "bound_conditionaccuracy > bound_conditionspeed")
```

Both tests provide strong evidence for selective influence. The Savage-Dickey Bayes Factor for drift being higher for words than nonwords is BF = `r round(t1_bf_drift, 1)`, and the Bayes Factor for bound being higher under accuracy than speed emphasis is BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t1_bf_bound), "\\\\infty", round(t1_bf_bound, 1))` — confirming that the difficulty manipulation affected drift specifically and the emphasis manipulation affected bound specifically.

# Tutorial 2: Estimating Response Bias with the EZ-Diffusion Model (4par)

Tutorial 1 used accuracy coding, where "upper" means correct regardless of stimulus type. But what if we want to know whether participants are biased toward saying "word"? Response bias is a substantively important question in many domains: in lexical decision, word frequency creates an a priori expectation that biases responses toward "word"; in recognition memory, participants may adopt liberal or conservative response criteria; in clinical research, impulsive responding in ADHD may manifest as a shifted starting point rather than changed drift. To estimate such biases, we need *response coding* — where "upper" always means a "word" response — and the 4-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model (`ezdm` 4par), which adds the relative starting point ($\zeta$) as a fourth parameter.^[The companion script `scripts/12_tutorial2_ezdm_4par.R` provides additional code for the simulated 4par validation.]

## What Changes

Switching from accuracy coding to response coding changes the question the model answers. Under accuracy coding, the model asks: "How quickly does evidence accumulate toward the *correct* answer?" Under response coding, it asks: "How quickly does evidence accumulate toward saying *word*?" These are different questions that lead to different parameter interpretations.

Specifically, drift now reflects evidence toward saying "word" — positive for word stimuli (lexical evidence supports the "word" response), negative for nonwords (lexical evidence opposes it). Boundary separation and non-decision time retain their interpretations, but the key new parameter is the relative starting point $\zeta$: values above 0.5 indicate a tendency to say "word" before evidence accumulation has run its course — an *a priori response bias* that the accuracy-coded model could not detect.

Estimating $\zeta$ requires separate summary statistics for upper- and lower-boundary responses. The 4-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model identifies the starting point from the asymmetry in these boundary-specific RT moments.

```{r}
#| label: t2-model
model_resp <- ezdm(
  mean_rt  = c("mean_rt_upper", "mean_rt_lower"),
  var_rt   = c("var_rt_upper", "var_rt_lower"),
  n_upper  = "n_upper",
  n_trials = "n_trials",
  version  = "4par"
)

formula_resp_ezdm <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stim_cat + (0 + stim_cat | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: t2-fit
fit_resp_ezdm <- bmm(
  formula = formula_resp_ezdm,
  data    = data_resp_ezdm,
  model   = model_resp,
  chains  = 5,
  cores   = 5,
  warmup  = 1000,
  iter    = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12),
  file    = here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp")
)
```

## Trial-Count Constraint

An important practical consideration: the `ezdm` 4par version requires sufficient trials on *both* boundaries in every cell. In this dataset, nonword stimuli under accuracy emphasis yield very few "word" responses (median: 17, minimum: 1), making variance estimates for the minority boundary unreliable. This is a genuine limitation of the EZ-Diffusion 4par approach that arises organically with real data. Tutorial 3 introduces trial-level models that handle this through hierarchical shrinkage.

## Results

Convergence was adequate (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t2_rhat, 3)`). A posterior predictive check confirms adequate model fit (@fig-t2-ppcheck).

```{r}
#| label: fig-t2-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check for the EZ-Diffusion 4par model fitted to the response-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "12_pp_check.pdf"))
```

As expected, drift reverses by stimulus category: positive for word stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t2_drift_word`, evidence accumulates toward the "word" boundary) and negative for nonword stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t2_drift_nonword`, evidence accumulates toward the "nonword" boundary). This sign reversal is a direct consequence of response coding — the same underlying evidence accumulation process is now expressed relative to the "word" boundary rather than the "correct" boundary. The $\zeta$ estimates reveal a small starting-point shift: $\zeta$ = `r t2_zr_acc_ci` under accuracy emphasis and $\zeta$ = `r t2_zr_speed_ci` under speed emphasis. The accuracy-emphasis estimate of `r t2_zr_acc` suggests a slight bias toward saying "word," while the speed-emphasis estimate of `r t2_zr_speed` is close to unbiased. These values are consistent with the original @wagenmakers2008lexical analysis ($\zeta$ = 0.497 for accuracy, 0.476 for speed), confirming that this dataset shows only a very small a priori response bias (@fig-t2-params).

```{r}
#| label: fig-t2-params
#| fig-cap: "EZ-Diffusion 4par parameter estimates from the response-coded analysis. Left: Drift estimates by stimulus category — positive for word stimuli, negative for nonword stimuli. Middle: Bound estimates by emphasis condition. Right: Relative starting point by emphasis condition — values near 0.5 indicate minimal response bias."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "12_resp_params.pdf"))
```

Hypothesis tests confirm the expected patterns. The Bayes Factor for drift being positive for words is BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t2_bf_drift_word), "$\\infty$", round(t2_bf_drift_word, 1))`, and for drift being negative for nonwords BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t2_bf_drift_nw), "$\\infty$", round(t2_bf_drift_nw, 1))`. The Bayes Factor for bound being higher under accuracy than speed emphasis is BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t2_bf_bound), "$\\infty$", round(t2_bf_bound, 1))` — the selective influence pattern is robust to the change in response coding.

The trial-count constraint discussed above is not merely a technical inconvenience — it highlights a fundamental limitation of summary-statistic approaches. When some cells contain very few responses on one boundary, the per-cell variance estimates that the EZ-Diffusion Model requires become unreliable. Trial-level models address this through hierarchical shrinkage: rather than computing per-cell statistics, they estimate parameters from the full RT distribution while borrowing strength across participants. We turn to the first trial-level model next.

# Tutorial 3: Trial-Level Modeling with the Censored-Shifted Wald

So far, the EZ-Diffusion Model has worked with summary statistics — three numbers per cell. But what if we need to model individual RTs? Trial-level modeling preserves distributional information, allows trial-level predictors, and — critically — handles sparse cells through hierarchical shrinkage rather than requiring stable per-cell variance estimates. The Censored-Shifted Wald provides this trial-level capability while remaining substantially faster than the full DDM.^[The companion script `scripts/13_tutorial3_cswald.R` provides additional code for the simulated Censored-Shifted Wald validation.]

## The Censored-Shifted Wald Architecture

Why not jump directly to the DDM? The DDM's Wiener likelihood, while mathematically complete, involves evaluating an infinite series for every trial — making it computationally expensive for iterative model development. The Censored-Shifted Wald sidesteps this by using the shifted Wald distribution, which describes the first-passage time of a diffusion process to a single absorbing boundary [@anders2016shifted; @heathcote2004fitting]. This single-boundary process is simpler to evaluate, yielding fitting times several times shorter than the full DDM (a few hours rather than the better part of a day on the present dataset). When error rates are low, the shifted Wald closely approximates the full two-boundary DDM (see DDM Estimation Approaches in the Background section), making the Censored-Shifted Wald a practical tool for developing and refining trial-level models before committing to the DDM's computational cost. Importantly, the `bmm` workflow remains identical — the only changes are the model object (`cswald()` instead of `ezdm()`) and the data format (trial-level RT and response columns instead of aggregated summary statistics).

## Simple Version: Accuracy-Coded Analysis

When most responses are correct, errors are relatively rare events. Rather than modeling the full two-boundary decision process, the *simple* Censored-Shifted Wald treats errors as cases where the accumulation process was interrupted before reaching the correct boundary — a *censoring* approach borrowed from survival analysis. This is appropriate when error rates are below approximately 20% [@miller2018shifted]. In the present dataset, accuracy-coded error rates range from 4% (nonwords, accuracy emphasis) to 19% (words, speed emphasis) — well within the simple version's range.

```{r}
#| label: t3-model-simple
model_simple <- cswald(
  rt       = "rt",
  response = "response",
  version  = "simple"
)

formula_simple <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stim_cat + (0 + stim_cat | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: t3-fit-simple
fit_cswald_simple <- bmm(
  formula = formula_simple,
  data    = data_accuracy_clean,
  model   = model_simple,
  chains  = 5,
  cores   = 5,
  warmup  = 1000,
  iter    = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12),
  file    = here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_simple")
)
```

The model converged well (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t3_rhat_simple, 3)`). The simple version models a single absorbing boundary by treating errors as censored observations; in the `bmm` parameterization, its bound estimates align closely with the EZ-Diffusion Model and the published reference values (see Cross-Approach Comparison), so they can be read on a comparable scale. Because the single-boundary approximation is least faithful for boundary separation, drift and ndt are the parameters the simple version recovers most reliably. The posterior predictive check (@fig-t3-ppcheck-simple) confirms adequate fit to the accuracy-coded RT distributions. The Censored-Shifted Wald (simple) recovers the same selective influence pattern as the EZ-Diffusion Model: drift is higher for words ($\delta$ = `r t3s_drift_word`) than nonwords ($\delta$ = `r t3s_drift_nonword`; BF = `r round(t3_bf_drift, 1)`), and bound is higher under accuracy emphasis (`r t3s_bound_acc`) than speed emphasis (`r t3s_bound_speed`; BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t3_bf_bound), "$\\infty$", round(t3_bf_bound, 1))`).

```{r}
#| label: fig-t3-ppcheck-simple
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check for the Censored-Shifted Wald (simple) model fitted to the accuracy-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "13_pp_check_simple.pdf"))
```

## Competing-Risks Version: Response-Coded Analysis

The *competing-risks* (crisk) version takes a different approach: instead of censoring errors, it models them explicitly through two independent racing accumulators — one for each response boundary — that share the same non-decision time. This allows estimation of the relative starting point $\zeta$. We apply it to the response-coded data, where it can estimate $\zeta$ and handle the unbalanced boundary counts that limited the EZ-Diffusion 4par approach.

```{r}
#| label: t3-model-crisk
model_crisk <- cswald(
  rt       = "rt",
  response = "response",
  version  = "crisk"
)

formula_crisk <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stim_cat + (0 + stim_cat | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: t3-fit-crisk
fit_cswald_crisk <- bmm(
  formula = formula_crisk,
  data    = data_response_clean,
  model   = model_crisk,
  chains  = 5,
  cores   = 5,
  warmup  = 1000,
  iter    = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12),
  file    = here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_resp")
)
```

The crisk model also converged well (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t3_rhat_crisk, 3)`). The posterior predictive check (@fig-t3-ppcheck-crisk) confirms adequate fit. The crisk version recovers the drift sign reversal seen in the EZ-Diffusion 4par and estimates $\zeta$ values close to 0.5 ($\zeta$ = `r t3c_zr_acc` under accuracy emphasis, `r t3c_zr_speed` under speed emphasis) — consistent with both the EZ-Diffusion 4par results and the original analysis.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t3-ppcheck-crisk
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check for the Censored-Shifted Wald (competing-risks) model fitted to the response-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "13_pp_check_crisk.pdf"))
```

## When to Use Which Version

The simple version is appropriate when error rates are low (<20%) and the research question does not require estimating $\zeta$. It is faster to fit and produces drift and ndt estimates on an interpretable scale, though bound represents half the full boundary separation. The crisk version is needed when error rates are higher, when $\zeta$ is of interest, or when response coding is used. One known limitation of the crisk version: it systematically underestimates bound by approximately 10% relative to the DDM. This is an inherent property of the competing-risks approximation — the two independent racing accumulators do not perfectly reproduce the dynamics of a single accumulator drifting between two boundaries. In practice, this means that if a researcher's primary question concerns boundary separation — for example, whether a clinical group shows reduced response caution — the Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk) may underestimate group differences. For drift-focused research questions, however, the Censored-Shifted Wald produces estimates that closely match the full DDM (as we confirm in the Cross-Model Comparison).

# Tutorial 4: Full DDM Likelihood Estimation

The Censored-Shifted Wald provides an efficient trial-level approach, but its single-boundary approximation does not fully capture the dynamics of the two-boundary decision process — as reflected in the systematic bound underestimation. For confirmatory analyses where the most accurate parameter estimates are needed, full DDM likelihood estimation is the gold standard. By jointly modeling the complete RT distribution for both correct and error responses within a single likelihood — no approximations, no censoring — the full DDM provides the most faithful implementation of the diffusion model framework. In this tutorial, we increase model complexity by using the full four-level `freq` variable (high-frequency words, low-frequency words, very-low-frequency words, nonwords) on drift, matching the specification of @wagenmakers2008lexical.^[The companion script `scripts/14_tutorial4_ddm.R` contains the full executable code.]

## DDM on Accuracy-Coded Data

In accuracy coding, all drifts are positive — they measure evidence toward the correct boundary regardless of stimulus type. An important consequence is that the drift rank order differs from the response-coded model: high-frequency words have the highest drift, but nonwords (which are relatively easy to reject) have higher drift than very-low-frequency words (which are difficult to recognize). The expected rank order, based on the reference values from @wagenmakers2008lexical (converted to $s = 1$), is: HF (4.52) > LF (2.75) > NW (2.64) > VLF (1.80).

```{r}
#| label: t4-model-acc
model_ddm <- ddm(rt = "rt", response = "response")

formula_ddm_acc <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)

fit_ddm_acc <- bmm(
  formula = formula_ddm_acc,
  data    = data_accuracy_clean,
  model   = model_ddm,
  chains  = 5,
  cores   = 5,
  warmup  = 1000,
  iter    = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12),
  file    = here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_acc")
)
```

## DDM on Response-Coded Data

In response coding, drift sign reflects the stimulus: positive for words (evidence accumulates toward the "word" boundary) and negative for nonwords. The expected values are: HF (4.52) > LF (2.75) > VLF (1.80) > 0 > NW (-2.64). The relative starting point $\zeta$ captures any bias toward saying "word"; the reference values suggest a very small shift between conditions ($\zeta$ = 0.497 accuracy, 0.476 speed).

```{r}
#| label: t4-model-resp
formula_ddm_resp <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
)

fit_ddm_resp <- bmm(
  formula = formula_ddm_resp,
  data    = data_response_clean,
  model   = model_ddm,
  chains  = 5,
  cores   = 5,
  warmup  = 1000,
  iter    = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12),
  file    = here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_resp")
)
```

Both DDM models converged (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t4_rhat_acc, 3)` for the accuracy-coded model, `r round(t4_rhat_resp, 3)` for the response-coded model). Posterior predictive checks (@fig-t4-ppcheck) confirm that the DDM captures the RT distributions well.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t4-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check for the DDM fitted to the accuracy-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "14_pp_check_acc.pdf"))
```

The accuracy-coded DDM recovers the expected drift rank ordering: HF (`r t4_drift_hf`) > NW (`r t4_drift_nw`) > LF (`r t4_drift_lf`) > VLF (`r t4_drift_vlf`). Boundary separation is clearly higher under accuracy emphasis ($\alpha$ = `r t4_bound_acc`) than speed emphasis ($\alpha$ = `r t4_bound_speed`), and non-decision time is estimated at $\tau$ = `r t4_ndt` s. As in the earlier tutorials, we can quantify the evidence for these effects with directional hypothesis tests: the frequency effect on drift (HF > VLF; BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t4_bf_drift), "$\\infty$", round(t4_bf_drift, 1))`) and the emphasis effect on bound (accuracy > speed; BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t4_bf_bound), "$\\infty$", round(t4_bf_bound, 1))`) are both supported decisively, reproducing the conclusions reached with the faster approaches. The response-coded DDM estimates starting point values close to 0.5 ($\zeta$ = `r t4_zr_acc` for accuracy, `r t4_zr_speed` for speed), consistent with the EZ-Diffusion 4par and Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk) results.

Fitting the full DDM took substantially longer than the EZ-Diffusion Model (~30 seconds) or Censored-Shifted Wald (~4–5 hours for the simple version): approximately 18–20 hours per model on the present dataset (wall-clock time with five chains run in parallel). We set `adapt_delta = 0.90` and `max_treedepth = 12` for both the Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM to reduce divergent transitions and max-treedepth warnings; these settings are recommended as defaults for trial-level DDM fitting.

## The EZ-Diffusion Model as a Fast Alternative

Given the substantial computational cost of the full DDM, a natural question is whether the EZ-Diffusion Model can produce comparable results with the same model specification. To test this, we fitted the EZ-Diffusion Model with the identical four-level `freq` variable on drift — both accuracy-coded (3par) and response-coded (4par). Summary statistics were computed using the mixture method for the 3par model and the robust method for the 4par model, which avoids convergence issues in sparse cells (e.g., nonword stimuli under accuracy emphasis yield very few "word" responses).

```{r}
#| label: t4-ezdm-comparison
#| eval: false
# EZDM 3par with freq (accuracy-coded) — see companion script for full code
data_acc_ezdm_freq <- data_accuracy_clean |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(rt, response, version = "3par",
                       method = "mixture", distribution = "exgaussian"),
    .by = c(id, condition, freq)
  )

fit_ezdm_freq <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(
    drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
    bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
    ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
  ),
  data = data_acc_ezdm_freq,
  model = ezdm(mean_rt = "mean_rt", var_rt = "var_rt",
               n_upper = "n_upper", n_trials = "n_trials", version = "3par"),
  # ... same fitting settings as above
)

# EZDM 4par with freq (response-coded)
data_resp_ezdm_freq <- data_response_clean |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(rt, response, version = "4par",
                       method = "robust", min_trials = 3),
    .by = c(id, condition, freq)
  )

fit_ezdm_resp_freq <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(
    drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
    bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
    ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
    zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
  ),
  data = data_resp_ezdm_freq,
  model = ezdm(mean_rt = c("mean_rt_upper", "mean_rt_lower"),
               var_rt = c("var_rt_upper", "var_rt_lower"),
               n_upper = "n_upper", n_trials = "n_trials", version = "4par"),
  # ... same fitting settings as above
)
```

Both EZ-Diffusion models converged in under three minutes — several hundred times faster than the full DDM. @fig-ezdm-vs-ddm compares the parameter estimates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ezdm-vs-ddm
#| fig-cap: "EZ-Diffusion vs. full DDM parameter estimates for the accuracy-coded analysis with four frequency levels on drift. Left: Drift estimates by frequency level — the EZ-Diffusion Model produces qualitatively identical rank orderings with slightly higher absolute values. Middle: Bound estimates by condition — the EZ-Diffusion Model underestimates bound relative to the full DDM, particularly under accuracy emphasis. Right: Non-decision time — the EZ-Diffusion Model estimates higher ndt than the full DDM. X markers show reference values from Wagenmakers et al. (2008)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "14_ezdm_vs_ddm_freq.pdf"))
```

The comparison reveals a systematic pattern. The EZ-Diffusion Model recovers the same drift rank ordering as the full DDM (HF > NW > LF > VLF in accuracy coding), with drift estimates approximately `r t4_drift_pct_mean`% higher on average (ranging from `r t4_drift_pct_lo`% to `r t4_drift_pct_hi`% across frequency levels) — consistent with the known attenuation of EZ-Diffusion drift estimates at high values [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. The EZ-Diffusion Model underestimates bound relative to the full DDM, particularly under accuracy emphasis where the DDM uses the full RT distribution shape to inform boundary separation. Non-decision time is estimated higher by the EZ-Diffusion Model ($\tau$ = `r t4_ndt_ez` s) than the full DDM ($\tau$ = `r t4_ndt_ddm` s), likely because the EZ-Diffusion Model absorbs some decision-time variability into ndt. For the response-coded 4par model, the EZ-Diffusion Model also recovered the drift sign reversal (positive for words, negative for nonwords) and estimated $\zeta$ values consistent with the full DDM.

These results demonstrate that the EZ-Diffusion Model is not merely a rough screening tool but a viable estimation approach in its own right. When the research question centers on drift — which experimental factor affects which cognitive process, and in what direction — the EZ-Diffusion Model provides the same substantive conclusions as the full DDM at a fraction of the computational cost. This computational cost motivates the staged workflow described in the Practical Guidelines.

# Cross-Approach Comparison

Having applied all three DDM estimation approaches to the same empirical dataset, we can now evaluate a question that is difficult to answer without a unified framework: when do the models agree, and where do approximations break down? Agreement validates the faster models against the gold-standard DDM; disagreement reveals where the computational savings come at a substantive cost.

## Accuracy-Coded Estimates

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison-acc
#| fig-cap: "Cross-model comparison of accuracy-coded parameter estimates. All three estimation approaches (EZ-Diffusion, Censored-Shifted Wald simple, full DDM) converge on the same selective influence pattern: stimulus category affects drift while emphasis condition affects bound."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_cross_model_accuracy.pdf"))
```

@fig-comparison-acc shows the accuracy-coded parameter estimates side by side. All three estimation approaches converge on the same *selective influence* pattern: stimulus category affects drift while emphasis condition affects bound. This convergence is reassuring — the core substantive conclusion holds regardless of whether we use summary statistics (EZ-Diffusion), a single-boundary approximation (Censored-Shifted Wald), or the full Wiener likelihood (DDM).

The approaches diverge in absolute values in ways consistent with their known properties (@tbl-cross-model-acc reports the parameters all three share). The EZ-Diffusion Model produces higher drift estimates than the trial-level approaches — around `r t4_drift_pct_mean`% higher on the frequency scale and more pronounced on the collapsed stimulus-category scale — consistent with the known attenuation of EZ-Diffusion drift at high values [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. For boundary separation, the EZ-Diffusion and Censored-Shifted Wald (simple) estimates agree closely with each other and with the published reference values, while the full DDM estimates somewhat higher boundaries, most visibly under accuracy emphasis, where it draws on the full RT-distribution shape. Non-decision time shows a clear ordering (@tbl-cross-model-acc): the EZ-Diffusion Model estimates higher ndt than the trial-level approaches, likely because it absorbs some decision-time variability that the distributional likelihoods of the full DDM and Censored-Shifted Wald capture directly.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cross-model-acc
#| tbl-cap: "Accuracy-coded parameter estimates (posterior mean [95% CrI], natural scale) for the parameters the three approaches share: boundary separation by emphasis condition and non-decision time. Bound and ndt are back-transformed from the log link. Drift is compared in @fig-comparison-acc and @fig-ezdm-vs-ddm."
#| echo: false
.g3 <- function(fe, row, d = 2) fmt_est(exp(fe[row, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), d)
cross_tab_acc <- tibble::tibble(
  Parameter = c("Bound, speed ($\\alpha$)", "Bound, accuracy ($\\alpha$)", "ndt ($\\tau$, s)"),
  `EZ-Diffusion`    = c(.g3(fe_t1,  "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t1,  "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t1,  "ndt_Intercept", 3)),
  `CSWALD (simple)` = c(.g3(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t3s, "ndt_Intercept", 3)),
  `Full DDM`        = c(.g3(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t4a, "ndt_Intercept", 3))
)
knitr::kable(cross_tab_acc, align = "lccc")
```

## Response-Coded Estimates

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison-resp
#| fig-cap: "Cross-approach comparison of response-coded parameter estimates. Left: Drift estimates by stimulus category — all three approaches show positive drift for words and negative drift for nonwords. Right: Relative starting point by emphasis condition — all three approaches estimate values close to 0.5.
```
